say.text: A cyanotic infant has TOF. The right ventricle faces a narrowed outflow, and the VSD gives blood another exit.
Predict the lung fields on the chest X-ray.

choices.label: Plethoric: the VSD floods the lungs

say.text: Compare the two exits for right ventricular blood: the narrowed outflow, or the VSD leading to the aorta. Which is easier, and what does that leave for the lungs?
Yes. With significant RVOT (right ventricular outflow tract) obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the pulmonary bed.
That is why the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings, **pulmonary oligaemia**.
Tempting, because a VSD alone is a left-to-right shunt that floods the lungs. Here the outflow obstruction changes the direction of flow.
With significant RVOT obstruction most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed, so markings are decreased (**oligaemia**).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the obstruction, not the VSD, decides where the blood goes.

say.text: Tempting, because a thick, strained ventricle sounds like a big heart. The claims say otherwise for this film.
The film shows decreased pulmonary markings, and StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the size too: normal-size silhouette, oligaemic lungs.

say.text: Same child, same obstruction. The right ventricle has pushed against it for months.
Which ECG fits?

choices.label: Left axis deviation with an LVH pattern
Right axis deviation with an RVH pattern

say.text: Ask which ventricle is pumping against the obstruction, and which side of the heart that ventricle sits on.
Yes. The ECG shows right axis deviation, prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1, characteristic of right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.
The hypertrophy is a consequence of chronic systemic pressures, not a primary defect.
Tempting, because 'ventricular hypertrophy' without a side sounds like the left ventricle, the usual pump.
In TOF the ECG shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy, because the right ventricle faces the obstruction.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the side now: RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures in the right ventricle.

say.text: Tempting, because left-sided enlargement is the familiar answer to a strained heart.
The TOF ECG shows right axis deviation, with R or qR waves in V1 characteristic of right atrial enlargement and RVH. It is right-sided.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the side: right atrium and right ventricle, not left.

say.text: That same thick right ventricle shows on the chest film as an upturned apex, the 'boot-shaped' heart.
What lifts the apex?
Yes. The upturned apex is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy, together with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.
Tempting, because a big pulmonary artery sounds like a bulge on the film. Here the main pulmonary artery segment is the opposite.
It is concave, and the upturned apex comes from right ventricular hypertrophy.
Tempting, because the left ventricle is the chamber most often blamed for heart shape.
The upturned apex of the boot-shaped heart is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy.
Tempting, because left atrial size changes the cardiac outline in other conditions. That is not this mechanism.
The apex is upturned by right ventricular hypertrophy.
Now the wording. A colleague says: 'No boot-shaped heart on the film, so it cannot be TOF.'
Which statement matches the source?

choices.label: The boot shape is present in every TOF film
It may classically be seen; the wording is not 'always'
It is the sign that confirms TOF on a film

say.text: Re-read the source phrase for this sign: radiographs may ... what? Look at the verb and the adverb.
Yes. Chest radiographs **may classically** show a boot-shaped heart with an upturned apex due to RVH. 'May classically' is a qualifier, not 'always'.
Tempting, because a classic sign gets remembered as a rule. The source wording is weaker.
Radiographs may classically show the boot shape. That is not the same as always present.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the qualifier: 'may classically'.

say.text: Tempting, because the boot is the best-known film sign. A film sign does not confirm the diagnosis.
The source says radiographs may classically show it; the echocardiogram is the gold standard.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two jobs: the film may show a classic sign, echo is the gold standard.

say.text: Put the film together. Which description fits TOF?

choices.label: Normal-sized heart, upturned apex, oligaemic lungs
Egg-on-a-string heart with a narrow pedicle

say.text: Yes. StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex, and the film can show pulmonary oligaemia.
Tempting, because shunt lesions often enlarge the heart and flood the lungs. That is not the TOF picture.
The TOF film shows a normal-size silhouette and decreased pulmonary markings.
Tempting, because it is a named film sign from the cyanotic heart disease list. Matching names from a list is the risk; build the TOF film from its mechanism.
TOF: normal-size silhouette, upturned apex, concave pulmonary segment, decreased markings.
ECG and film point to TOF, but they only suggest it. The team needs the test that confirms.
Which is the gold standard for diagnosis?
Ask which test answers 'what is the diagnosis?' without a catheter, contrast or a long scan, and shows the anatomy directly.
Yes. The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary diagnostic modality.
It allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy.
Tempting, because catheterisation is invasive and detailed, and invasive feels definitive. The question is about diagnosis, not detail.
The echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis of TOF.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so rank tests by the question they answer, not by invasiveness.

say.text: Tempting, because CT gives crisp images. Its job is different.
Contrast-enhanced CT is useful for demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology; the gold standard for diagnosis is echo.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember CT's job is morphology, not diagnosis.

say.text: Echo has confirmed TOF. Before repair the team wants the complex cardiovascular morphology shown in detail.
What adds this?
Yes. Contrast-enhanced CT is useful in demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology of TOF.

choices.label: Go deeper: where echo falls short

say.text: Tempting, because echo is the primary modality, so it seems to need no partner.
Echo is the primary diagnostic modality, but CT is useful for the complex morphology, so the tests have different jobs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match each test to one job: echo diagnoses, CT shows morphology.

say.text: Tempting, because catheterisation was once the detailed test. It is not the gold standard.
The echocardiogram is the gold standard; CT adds morphology.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reset: echo diagnoses, CT shows morphology.

say.text: Echo has limits for extracardiac anomalies such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia.
Assessing the pulmonary arteries matters: repairing the cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome.
Last rung. Which pairing of test and job is right in TOF?

choices.label: MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo only for follow-up
Catheterisation for diagnosis; echo for screening only
Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function, no radiation

say.text: Yes. Echo is the primary diagnostic modality, and MRI gives both anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.
Tempting, because MRI gives so much detail. Detail does not make it first-line.
Echo is the primary modality for diagnosis; MRI adds anatomy and function without radiation.
Tempting, because screening sounds like a small job for echo. It is the gold standard.
Echo is the gold standard and the primary modality for diagnosis.
The ladder: the RV faces the block, so the ECG is right-sided (RAD, RVH) and the film is oligaemic with an upturned apex that may classically look boot-shaped.
Echo diagnoses, CT shows morphology, MRI adds function.
